description: We are a multidisciplinary team combining Software Engineering, Business Administration and Electrical Engineering. Our goal is to help farmers in rural Spain make better planting decisions: SovrHarvest uses NASA Earth observation data (NASA POWER, GPM IMERG and MODIS) to show farmers which legume could improve their rotation, how much it could earn and how much it risks. By reducing dependence on imported fertilizer and protein, it also contributes to Europe’s food resilience.
summary:
SovrHarvest helps farmers choose which legume to add to their rotation, using NASA data for their own field.

In 2026 cereal output in Castilla y León, Spain’s main cereal region, fell 42% while the average cost of fertilizers rose 22%. Most farms grow wheat and barley year after year, relying on costly nitrogen. Legumes like peas, lentils or chickpeas can replace part of it and restore the soil, but farmers can’t tell which one suits their field or if it pays off.

The farmer enters the official parcel ID (SIGPAC) or taps the field on a map. The app gathers 2000-2026 data for that field from NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, MODIS and SoilGrids, drops legumes the soil can’t support and replays the last 15 seasons. Each option is scored on money earned vs. the current rotation, climate risk and soil fit, explained in plain language. MODIS shows how reliable the result is by checking if the field gets less green after dry springs.

What’s next for SovrHarvest? SIGPAC covers all of Spain, so we will extend SovrHarvest nationwide. Then we will go beyond legumes: by tracking how each field’s climate and soil change over the years, it will detect land now suited to new crops, like areas of Tarragona becoming good for vineyards.

Impact: NASA data turned into a clear answer on what to plant, whether it pays off and what it puts at risk.
details:
How it works

SovrHarvest builds on the parcel data from SIGPAC and the crops the farmer grew in the last three seasons. From the NASA data it calculates, for every season, the weather that matters to a crop: autumn and spring rain, heat days in May, hard winter frosts and late spring frosts.

It first discards legumes the soil cannot support, such as lupin on limestone soils. Then it tests six legumes (pea, lentil, chickpea, bitter vetch, lupin and vetch-oat forage), each in a legume–wheat–barley rotation, and the farmer’s current rotation with exactly the same method. For each of the last 15 seasons it estimates the yield from that year’s real weather, multiplies it by real market prices and subtracts production costs. It also adds the fertilizer the legume saves for the next cereal (at the current urea price) and the EU farm subsidy (CAP) eco-scheme payment for rotations.

Beyond the recommendation, the web includes:

“What if I had started 15 years ago?”: a chart of how much more, or less, the farmer would have earned season by season.

Fertilizer price scenarios (−30% to +60%, as in 2022), to see if the recommendation holds when prices change.

Current disease risk near the farm: NASA POWER temperature and humidity from the last two weeks, compared with the previous ten years.

Field tools: a map of the legumes grown in each province, a comparison between two fields, a season-by-season plan and a printable report.

Benefits and impact

Farmers get a field-specific answer in plain language without accounts, sensors or technical knowledge, using a parcel ID they already know from their subsidy forms. Legumes cut fertilizer costs and dependence on synthetic nitrogen, which also lowers emissions, and they improve soil health. Our first goal is to help Castilla y León farmers recover after a disastrous year. The method is generic and can be extended to other rainfed regions with their own crops, prices and parcel registry.

Tools

Code: Python with FastAPI, Uvicorn, requests, h5py and pytest; HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet for the maps.

Map layers: IGN aerial imagery (PNOA), OpenStreetMap and the official SIGPAC parcel layer.

Other data: official yields and costs (Junta de Castilla y León, Spanish Ministry of Agriculture), prices from Spanish grain exchanges and disease conditions from ITACyL, the regional agricultural institute.

Team: three members working on GitHub, one on data collection, one on the decision engine and one on the interface, linked by a shared JSON data contract. No hardware beyond our laptops.

Creativity

It replays the farmer’s own past instead of guessing the future.

It works at field level, not on regional averages.

It uses NASA satellites to check its own model.

It is transparent: every rule, price and threshold is in the code with its source, and values without one are marked as estimates.

It adjusts each legume’s yield to its province, and it uses the higher market price for lentil grown in the La Armuña protected-origin area.

Factors we considered

Data resolution: we use each source for what it can measure reliably.

Crop-specific risks: pea and vetch suffer in dry springs, chickpea gets disease in very wet ones, and lentil and chickpea are harvested close to the ground, so steep fields are penalized.

Real economics: prices with their date and source, always compared with what the farmer already does.

The user: plain language and simple good/fair/poor ratings.

Honesty: the app supports the decision but does not replace a local agronomist. It says what data is missing and what to check with a technician.
